To give credence to something means to believe it, or to accept it as true and worthy of trust.

Think of "credence" as simply meaning belief or trust. So when you "give credence to" something, you are giving your belief to it — you are deciding it is real, valid, or trustworthy.
The Word "Credence" — Where It Comes From

Understanding the root of the word makes the idiom stick in your memory forever.

"Credence" comes from the Latin word credere, which means "to believe." This same Latin root gave us many English words you already know:

  • Credible — something believable
  • Incredible — something unbelievable (literally: "cannot be believed")
  • Credentials — proof that makes you worth trusting
  • Credit — trust given to someone financially
  • Creed — a system of beliefs

So the entire family of these words is built on the idea of believing or trusting. "Credence" is simply the noun form — it is the belief itself. When you give credence, you are handing over your trust or belief to something.
Two Slightly Different Ways It's Used

This idiom works in two directions, and both are very common. This is important to understand.

Direction 1 — A Person Gives Credence to Something

Here, a person (or a group of people) is choosing to believe something.

Structure: [Someone] gives credence to [a claim, idea, or theory]

Examples:

  • "I don't give credence to rumors."
    → I do not believe rumors. I don't trust them.
  • "She refused to give credence to his excuses."
    → She did not accept his excuses as true or valid.
  • "Many people gave credence to the scientist's warnings."
    → Many people believed the scientist's warnings were real and serious.

In this use, it describes an active mental choice — a person deciding whether or not to believe something.

Direction 2 — Something Gives Credence to Something Else

Here, a piece of evidence, a fact, or an event makes another thing seem more believable. No person is directly doing the believing — instead, one thing is strengthening the believability of another.

Structure: [Something] gives credence to [a claim, idea, or theory]

Examples:

  • "The eyewitness testimony gives credence to his story."
    → The witness's account makes his story more believable and supported.
  • "The discovery of ancient tools gives credence to the theory that humans lived here thousands of years ago."
    → The discovery supports and validates that theory.
  • "His pale face and shaking hands gave credence to his claim of feeling sick."
    → His physical appearance made his claim of illness seem more believable.

In this use, think of it as one thing lending its weight to another — making it stand more firmly.
The Tone and Register of This Idiom

This is a formal and slightly elevated idiom. You would more commonly see or hear it in:

  • Journalism and news articles
  • Academic writing
  • Formal speeches or debates
  • Serious conversations about evidence, theories, or claims

In casual everyday conversation, people would more often simply say "I believe it" or "that supports it." So if you use this idiom, it gives your language a polished, educated quality.
The Negative Form — Very Common and Important

One of the most frequent ways this idiom appears is in the negative, especially with the word "don't" or "no."

  • "I don't give credence to this nonsense." → I simply don't believe it.
  • "We should give no credence to unverified claims." → We should not believe things that haven't been proven.
  • "Don't give credence to everything you read online." → Don't blindly believe everything online.

When used negatively, the phrase becomes a polite but firm way of dismissing something — saying it is not worth believing.

You will very often see the phrase "lend credence to" instead of "give credence to." They mean exactly the same thing. The only difference is the verb:

  • Give credence to → you are giving/granting belief
  • Lend credence to → you are lending/adding support to believability

Both are correct and interchangeable. "Lend credence to" is arguably even more common in formal writing when talking about evidence supporting a theory.

"The data lends credence to the hypothesis."
"The data gives credence to the hypothesis."

Both sentences are identical in meaning.
Words That Mean the Same Thing (Synonyms)

Depending on context, these phrases carry a similar meaning:

  • Give weight to — very similar; implies something is taken seriously
  • Lend credibility to — almost identical in meaning
  • Validate — to confirm something is true or acceptable
  • Support — to back up a claim
  • Corroborate — especially when evidence confirms something
  • Vouch for — to personally confirm something is trustworthy
  • Substantiate — to provide proof for a claim

If "give credence to" means to believe or support something, the opposites include:

  • Discredit — to damage the believability of something
  • Cast doubt on — to make something seem less believable
  • Dismiss — to reject something as unworthy of belief
  • Debunk — to expose something as false
  • Undermine — to weaken the support for something
Quick Summary You Can Always Return To

MeaningTo believe something, or to make something seem more believable
RootLatin credere = to believe
Used by a person"I give credence to her theory." = I believe her theory.
Used by evidence"This gives credence to her theory." = This makes her theory more believable.
Common negative use"Don't give credence to gossip." = Don't believe gossip.
Twin phrase"Lend credence to" = exactly the same meaning

If you ever forget the meaning, just remember:

Credence = Belief. To "give" it = to hand it over.

When you give credence to something, you are handing your belief over to it. When something gives credence to a theory, it is handing believability over to that theory.

That's the whole idiom — elegant, precise, and now completely yours.
